# [What Is Fabric IQ?! Microsoft Fabric’s NEW Ontology Explained](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XEyq1qL147M)

**Visibility**: Public
**Uploaded by**: [Guy in a Cube](https://www.youtube.com/@GuyInACube)
**Uploaded at**: 2026-02-18
**Published at**: 
**Length**: 08:12
**Views**: 45362
**Likes**: 631
**Category**: Science & Technology

## Description

```
🔥 Confused about Fabric IQ? You’re not alone.

When Fabric IQ was announced at Ignite, it looked powerful… but what does it actually DO?

In this video, we sit down with Devang Shah to break down what Fabric IQ really is inside Microsoft Fabric and why ontology might be the missing context layer your AI agents desperately need.

You’ll learn:

✔️ What Fabric IQ actually is
✔️ What an ontology means in Microsoft Fabric
✔️ How entity types and relationships work
✔️ How to bind ontology to Lakehouse & Eventhouse
✔️ Why AI agents need context (to avoid hallucinations!)
✔️ How knowledge graphs improve reasoning

Fabric IQ allows you to:

- Add meaning to your data
- Create reusable AI context
- Connect transactional, analytical, and real-time data
- Build a shared context layer for humans AND AI agents

⏱️ Timeline
00:00 – Intro
00:27 – What is Fabric IQ?
01:35 – Why ontology matters for AI
02:01 – Retail ontology example walkthrough
02:50 – Entity types & relationships explained
03:40 – Binding ontology to Lakehouse
04:10 – Real-time data with Eventhouse
05:05 – Ontology overview & instances
06:45 – 3 reasons you should care about Fabric IQ
07:45 – Should we do a "how to"?

👇 Should we bring Devang back for a full step-by-step setup tutorial? Let us know in the comments!


*******************

Yooo! 🙌 take your data skills to the next level and join fellow data professionals in our community THE CUBE: https://guyinacube.com

🌐 LET'S CONNECT!
Official website: https://guyinacube.com
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/guyinacube
Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/guyinacube
Instagram: https://instagram.com/guyinacube
Bluesky: https://bsky.app/profile/guyinacube.com
X: https://x.com/guyinacube

🎤 HOST
Marthe Moengen

#PowerBI #MCPServer #GitHubCopilot #ClaudeAI #GuyInACube
```

## Transcript

Yooo, what's up?
Were you like me?
Super excited when watching Ignite and seeing this new
shiny thing being released.
Fabric IQ.
But you're also confused just like me because I'm not sure
I understand what it was.
So today I brought with me my really, really good friend, Devang Shah.
Hey Marthe, how are you?
Ah, I'm good.
And I'm excited that you're here because you are a Fabric IQ expert.
We need some help understanding this.
So what is Fabric IQ?
So, you know, we have been working with data for a long time, and data by itself
does not mean a lot unless you apply some context, unless you apply some meaning.
And that meaning is what you as users, human users use it in terms of
reports, in terms of visualizations, to understand what you can do with data.
Now, this meaning and this context, et cetera, is also relevant in the
era of AI where we are in right now.
Also for the AI agents, because you know, as humans, we have our
experience, we have our knowledge.
We've been doing these things for a while.
So sometimes you look at the data and they understand like, yeah,
this is what the number means.
But agents by themselves may not understand that because they don't
have that acquired experience.
So ontology is a way to apply context meaning to the data that we all have,
and that is the all around us, in our enterprise world, in our data
platforms to make it understandable for human agents, so people like us,
but also for AI agents.
So it's kind of a shared context layer in Fabric that can be used by AI and
humans both so that we can all progress.
Okay.
That's interesting.
But you know what, I think I, I think I need to see it to really understand it.
So you know what we like to do at Guy in a Cube?
Enough of all this talking.
Let's just head over to the Devang's laptop.
Alright, let's do it.
Okay, here I am.
I have created a little retail ontology, so we are gonna start with what I have.
So, uh, when we think about an ontology in Fabric, there
are three important concepts.
So one is entity types.
These entity types are some common concepts like, you know, warehouse
store returns, region products, you know, something that we see in a
typical retail scenario all the time.
So, for example, here I have a warehouse.
Shipments apart from warehouses, shipments are created for particular orders, right?
So shipments actually fulfill orders that our customers are placing, and we wanna
send those shipments to those customers.
Shipments are also delivered to region, and if you go to region, then region
would have multiple other relationships.
Region would also be connected to the customer because
customers are located in region.
So this is kind of a representation of an ontology.
Which consists of entity types, which explain what those concepts
are and how do you model them.
And then all of these entity types are connected to other
entity types via relationships.
And these relationships also have meanings.
Shipment deliver to region, promotion in region, demand in region.
This is important if anyone is trying to understand what is happening in this
retail store or in this retail company.
And if there is all this description and meaning available.
On the entity.
Entity as well as on the relationship.
Then human agents or AI agents can also start to reason over this
data much better compared to just having two tables established joint
relationships, but not having a lot of meaning attached to it, right?
So we know that AI agents and LLMs tend to hallucinate if
they're not given enough context.
But now imagine if you can build all of this context closer to your data, you can
empower those agents to go reason better.
So what do I mean by closer to the data?
So here I have created my entity types.
Now, these entity types also can have properties and must have properties.
So if I look at the region.
Region has number of different properties like country code,
region, name, time zone.
But if you, for example, click on the order entity type, it has more data.
So it can have order ID or the status payment method.
So these are all the different properties that you can assign or that are relevant
for this particular entity type.
Now, where do these properties come from?
You see there are these lakehouse icons here.
So you actually bind your ontology to an underlying data
table or data store in Fabric.
So here I have bound this particular order entity type to a lakehouse table.
You can do some static bindings in case some properties are static in nature,
which are not changing with time.
But you may also have some entity types which actually might change with time.
So here I have another entity type called a shipment.
And shipment, as you can see, has some other properties which are
bound to a different data store.
In this case, it is bound to shipments, which is an event house.
Now, in this event house, I also have location data.
You know, because shipments move from point A to point B,
so you also have that live data.
So what ontology allows you to do is once you've built it out, you can bind it to
a Lakehouse table to get all the static properties and important attributes.
But you can also bind it to live data, real time data, because
live context is also important
when you want to start asking questions, when you want to understand
what's happening with your shipments.
If the shipments are getting late, which customers are gonna be impacted in case
the shipments are gonna get late so that you can notify those customers on time.
You know, think of all those cool questions that you want to answer,
where multiple different entities come together and you can reason
over it and get answers quickly.
This is what ontology allows you to do in a very meaningful way.
And I guess most people already have a lot of data inside of Fabric that should
have these relationships and contexts already set up between them, and that's
what ontology will help us with, right?
Indeed.
So if you have your Fabric and if you have your one lake, you must
be having some lakehouse tables.
You must be having some event house tables in case you're doing some real time stuff.
And if you have some domain concepts, you know, for example, if you're in
the marketing domain, if you're in the sales domain, if you're in the retail,
think about what are those 4, 5, 7 different concepts that you want to model.
Start adding entity types.
Start building your relationships.
Give it some really descriptive meanings.
If you want those LMS to not hallucinate, assign all the properties, give some
really good property names, map it to the tables, and once your ontology
is ready to go, you can actually go to overview, which will give
you a little bit of a perspective of what's there in your entity.
So for example, I have about 1600 instances of shipments.
I can see the underlying knowledge crafts, and it'll also build out all
of this quick overview of, you know, what was the in transit temperature.
For example, if you're sending some goods, which have to be in a frozen
container or in freezers, then you can also see what was the temperature,
what was the humidity percentage, what was a latitude, longitude.
So you have some quick overview of your ontology.
And if you want to go into the details, you also have this individual shipment id.
So you also have a quick overview of what shipments are in transit, what
shipments are delivered, and then if you want to start filtering it out,
you can choose a particular instance and then you will have that data for
that particular shipment as well.
So this is how easy it is to build an ontology, get a quick overview
for ontology, and then you can start consuming ontology, which are
multiple different ways and Fabric.
Okay.
That was really impressive.
Thank you for showing us Devang.
Why should I start caring about Fabric IQ and start using ontology?
I would say Marthe, there are three main reasons.
Number one, as I said, we all have a lot of data.
All of this data may be used as semantic models may be used as different kind
of facts and dimension joints and all the kind of reports that you might be
doing, but represent that as knowledge graph as advantages, and represent
that as an ontology, as an advantage, because reasoning becomes easier.
Number two, we are giving a lot of prompt instructions when we are training agents.
A lot of these prompt instructions is also that context that you are
giving each agent so that they also understand how to work with data.
You have an opportunity to bring this context closer to the data so
that any agent which is connecting to this data via ontology, can
benefit from the same context.
So, hey, you have reusable contacts.
You don't have to go and train every agent individually in
terms of problems and et cetera.
And number three, ontology also allows you to combine all of your transactional
data, analytical data or real time data, unstructured data, and make
LLMs as well as agents and us smarter and better so that we can help our
organizations make better decisions.
I learned so much from you today, Devang.
Thank you.
If you guys also want to know more, maybe we should invite Devang back
to really deep dive into ontology.
Maybe he can show us how to set it up?
Let us know in the comments below.
If you haven't already, make sure to subscribe to Guy in a Cube and check
out the other awesome videos that might be flowing above my head from
Adam, Patrick, and this Gal right here.
We're excited to see you guys in the next video.
Byyyye!
